title: What is the difference between Flink's DataSet API (batch, deprecated) and DataStream API (streaming/batch, recommended low-level API), and when do you use DataStream vs Table API/Flink SQL (DataStream for fine-grained control; Table API/SQL for declarative, SQL-like analytics)?
shortTitle: What is the difference between Flink's DataSet API and DataStream API, and when do you use DataStream vs Table API/Flink SQL

s1_definition.profdef: The DataSet API was Flink's original low-level API for bounded batch processing, modeling data as finite collections transformed by operators like map, filter, groupBy, and join, and it is now deprecated in favor of a unified model. The DataStream API is the recommended low-level API that handles both unbounded streaming and bounded batch through a single programming model, supporting event-time processing, watermarks, keyed state, and timers, with a batch execution mode for bounded inputs. Above the DataStream API sit the Table API and Flink SQL, the declarative layer where you express computations as relational operations or SQL over dynamic tables. You use the DataStream API when you need fine-grained control over state, timers, and custom operator logic, and you use the Table API or Flink SQL when you want concise, maintainable, SQL-like analytics.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the old DataSet API was like a machine built only for processing a fixed pile of yesterday's transactions overnight, a finished stack with a clear end. The bank has moved past it. The DataStream API is a newer machine that handles both a never-ending live feed of transactions and a fixed pile, using the same controls, and it lets an engineer wire up every detail by hand: custom memory for each customer, alarm timers, bespoke rules. The Table API and Flink SQL sit on top as a friendly control panel where an analyst just types the query they want, like total per branch, and the machine figures out the wiring. You use the hand-wiring when you need a custom mechanism no panel button offers, and you use the panel for everyday analytics.
s1_definition.oneliner: DataSet is the deprecated batch-only low-level API; DataStream is the recommended low-level API unifying streaming and batch with full control over state and timers; the Table API and Flink SQL are the declarative layer for SQL-like analytics, used when you do not need low-level control.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The DataSet API was Flink's original low-level API for bounded batch processing, modeling data as finite collections transformed by operators like map, filter, groupBy, and join, and it is now deprecated in favor of a unified model. The DataStream API is the recommended low-level API that handles both unbounded streaming and bounded batch through a single programming model, supporting event-time processing, watermarks, keyed state, and timers, with a batch execution mode for bounded inputs. Above the DataStream API sit the Table API and Flink SQL, the declarative layer where you express computations as relational operations or SQL over dynamic tables. You use the DataStream API when you need fine-grained control over state, timers, and custom operator logic, and you use the Table API or Flink SQL when you want concise, maintainable, SQL-like analytics.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the old DataSet API was like a machine built only for processing a fixed pile of yesterday's transactions overnight, a finished stack with a clear end. The bank has moved past it. The DataStream API is a newer machine that handles both a never-ending live feed of transactions and a fixed pile, using the same controls, and it lets an engineer wire up every detail by hand: custom memory for each customer, alarm timers, bespoke rules. The Table API and Flink SQL sit on top as a friendly control panel where an analyst just types the query they want, like total per branch, and the machine figures out the wiring. You use the hand-wiring when you need a custom mechanism no panel button offers, and you use the panel for everyday analytics.

**One line to remember:** DataSet is the deprecated batch-only low-level API; DataStream is the recommended low-level API unifying streaming and batch with full control over state and timers; the Table API and Flink SQL are the declarative layer for SQL-like analytics, used when you do not need low-level control.

sections.s2_technical:
The DataSet API was built for bounded data: you read a finite input, apply transformations such as map, flatMap, filter, groupBy, reduce, and join, and produce a finite result, with the runtime free to use batch-optimized execution like sort-merge joins and full-blocking shuffles because it knows the data ends. It had no concept of event time, watermarks, or continuous state, because batch data does not stream. Flink has deprecated the DataSet API because maintaining two separate APIs, one for batch and one for streaming, was redundant once the DataStream API gained a proper batch execution mode. The direction is one unified API.

The DataStream API is that unified low-level API. It models data as a possibly-unbounded stream and offers the full streaming toolkit: event-time and processing-time semantics, watermarks for handling out-of-order data, keyed state scoped per key with pluggable backends, event-time and processing-time timers, windows, and low-level primitives like ProcessFunction for arbitrary custom logic. Crucially it also has a batch execution mode: when the sources are bounded, you can set the runtime mode to BATCH and Flink executes the same DataStream program with batch optimizations, so one program and one API cover both worlds. This is why the DataStream API is the recommended low-level choice: it is strictly more capable than the DataSet API and future-proof.

The Table API and Flink SQL are the declarative layer built on top. The Table API is a fluent, language-integrated relational API in Java, Scala, or Python, and Flink SQL is standard SQL; both operate over dynamic tables and compile down to the same underlying runtime as the DataStream API. You choose between the layers by how much control you need. You pick the Table API or Flink SQL when the computation is relational, filters, projections, joins, aggregations, windows, and pattern matching, because the declarative form is far more concise, easier to read and maintain, and the optimizer can improve the plan; this is the right default for analytics. You drop to the DataStream API when you need something SQL cannot express cleanly: custom per-key state machines, data-dependent timers, bespoke windowing or triggering, complex event logic beyond MATCH_RECOGNIZE, or precise control over operator behavior. A common real pattern is mixing them: do the heavy relational work in SQL and convert to a DataStream for a custom ProcessFunction where needed, since Flink lets you convert between a Table and a DataStream. The senior nuances are these. First, for new projects do not use the DataSet API at all; use the DataStream API in batch mode for bounded jobs. Second, prefer the highest-level API that fits, because declarative code is cheaper to maintain and benefits from optimization, and only descend to the DataStream API for genuine low-level needs. Third, the batch execution mode on the DataStream API changes scheduling and state behavior, so understand that bounded mode may use different shuffle and failover strategies than streaming mode. Fourth, you can interleave the APIs within one job, using SQL for analytics and ProcessFunction for custom logic. Knowing that the DataSet API is legacy, that the DataStream API unifies batch and streaming, and precisely when to use the declarative layer versus the low-level API, is exactly what marks an engineer who understands Flink's modern architecture.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India needs a simple relational analytic, the total transaction amount per branch, which is a plain GROUP BY and is far easier and more maintainable expressed declaratively than as hand-wired operators. This is exactly the case for the Table API or Flink SQL.

Problem 2 — The same bank also needs a custom rule, flagging an account whose transactions exceed a dynamic per-account threshold that itself updates based on prior behavior, which requires per-key state and custom logic that SQL cannot express cleanly. This is exactly the case for the low-level DataStream API with a ProcessFunction.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that contrasts the declarative and low-level styles on the same data, and shows that the DataSet style is just the bounded case now subsumed by batch mode. We define a `Txn`, a `DeclarativeAggregator` that models the Table-API or SQL style of a concise GROUP BY branch SUM, and a `LowLevelFraudDetector` that models a DataStream ProcessFunction keeping per-account state and a dynamic threshold to flag outliers. An `ApiChoiceDemo` main class runs the same transactions through both, printing the declarative branch totals and the low-level fraud flags, so the when-to-use-which distinction is concrete.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is five transactions for two accounts across two branches, used first by the declarative aggregator and then by the low-level fraud detector.

Step 1. The declarative aggregator processes all transactions as a single relational GROUP BY branch SUM. Mumbai receives fifty thousand, thirty thousand, and ninety thousand, totaling one hundred seventy thousand. Delhi receives twelve thousand and eight thousand, totaling twenty thousand. This is the kind of concise analytic you would write as one SQL statement, which is why the Table API or Flink SQL is the right choice here.

Step 2. The low-level fraud detector begins. For the first Mumbai transaction, account SAV2001 has no stored threshold, so it starts at forty thousand. The fifty thousand transaction exceeds forty thousand, so it is flagged. The detector then adapts the account's threshold upward, to forty-eight thousand, because the rule says the threshold grows with behavior. This per-account evolving state is exactly what SQL cannot express cleanly.

Step 3. The first Delhi transaction for CUR3001 starts at the initial forty thousand threshold. Twelve thousand is under it, so it is fine, and CUR3001's threshold adapts to forty-eight thousand.

Step 4. The third transaction, thirty thousand for SAV2001, is compared to SAV2001's now-elevated threshold of forty-eight thousand. Thirty thousand is under it, so it is fine, and the threshold adapts again to about fifty-eight thousand.

Step 5. The fifth transaction, ninety thousand for SAV2001, is compared to SAV2001's threshold, now about sixty-nine thousand after the fourth-step adaptation. Ninety thousand exceeds it, so it is flagged. The detector ends with two fraud flags, both for SAV2001. The lesson is clear: the branch totals were a trivial declarative query, while the dynamic per-account threshold required low-level keyed state and custom logic, which is exactly the DataStream API's domain.

Final output:

```
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    === Declarative (use Table API / Flink SQL) ===
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    declarative GROUP BY branch SUM -> {MUMBAI=170000, DELHI=20000}
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    === Low-level (use DataStream ProcessFunction) ===
2024-01-01 00:00:00 WARNING FRAUD FLAG T1 account=SAV2001 amount=50000 > threshold=40000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    ok T2 amount=12000 <= threshold=40000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    ok T3 amount=30000 <= threshold=48000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    ok T4 amount=8000 <= threshold=48000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 WARNING FRAUD FLAG T5 account=SAV2001 amount=90000 > threshold=69000
2024-01-01 00:00:00 INFO    fraud flags = [FRAUD FLAG T1 account=SAV2001 amount=50000 > threshold=40000, FRAUD FLAG T5 account=SAV2001 amount=90000 > threshold=69000]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flink has a layered set of APIs, and the modern story is a unified one. The DataSet API was Flink's original low-level API for bounded batch processing, modeling data as finite collections with operators like map, groupBy, and join, and it had no concept of event time, watermarks, or continuous state because batch data does not stream. It is now deprecated, because maintaining a separate batch API became redundant once the DataStream API gained a proper batch execution mode. The DataStream API is the recommended low-level API: it unifies unbounded streaming and bounded batch in one programming model, with event-time and processing-time semantics, watermarks, keyed state, timers, windows, and low-level primitives like ProcessFunction, and by setting the runtime mode to batch it runs the same program over bounded data with batch optimizations. Above it sit the Table API and Flink SQL, the declarative layer that compiles down to the same runtime.

The choice between layers is about how much control I need. I use the Table API or Flink SQL whenever the computation is relational, filters, projections, joins, aggregations, windows, and pattern matching, because the declarative form is far more concise, easier to read and maintain, and the optimizer can improve the plan; this is my default for analytics. I drop to the DataStream API only when I need something SQL cannot express cleanly: a custom per-key state machine, data-dependent timers, bespoke windowing or triggering, or complex event logic beyond MATCH_RECOGNIZE. A common real pattern is to mix them, doing the heavy relational work in SQL and converting a Table to a DataStream for a custom ProcessFunction where needed, since Flink supports that conversion. The senior points I stress are that new projects should not use the DataSet API at all but use the DataStream API in batch mode for bounded jobs, that I always prefer the highest-level API that fits because declarative code is cheaper to maintain and benefits from optimization, and that batch execution mode changes scheduling and failover behavior so bounded and streaming modes are not identical under the hood.

At the National Bank of India this distinction was a daily decision. For the straightforward analytics, such as total transaction amount per branch, I wrote one Flink SQL GROUP BY statement, because it was trivial, readable, and the optimizer handled it, and there was no reason to hand-wire operators. But for a fraud rule that flagged transactions exceeding a dynamic per-account threshold that itself adapted based on the account's prior behavior, SQL could not express the evolving per-key state cleanly, so I used the DataStream API with a keyed ProcessFunction holding each account's threshold in keyed state and updating it after every transaction. I kept the relational aggregation in SQL and the custom rule in a ProcessFunction within the same overall pipeline, which is exactly the recommended mix. Being able to explain that the DataSet API is legacy, that the DataStream API unifies batch and streaming with full low-level control, and precisely when to reach for the declarative layer versus the low-level API, with a concrete example of each, is what shows I understand Flink's modern architecture rather than just one API.
